lessons: Ground the premise in an extreme contrast, paradox, or massive scale immediately (e.g. 'older than the United States', 'meat looks like two completely different animals', 'Kuiper belt extends much further'); videos with these conceptual extremes achieved the highest retention at 10% (>1.21) and vs_similar_start (>0.53).

Avoid immediate generic or mechanical explanations right after the hook; 20 out of 25 videos experience their largest drop between 8% and 19% when transitioning into dense exposition (e.g. sap water percentages, plant defense chemistry, cell nodes), losing 20-34% of viewers.

Do not insert interactive prompts or countdown pauses ('Pause and guess...', 'three, two, one'); countdown and guess lines trigger severe drops (e.g. 8.3% lost at 52% in Maple Syrup, 15.2% lost at 37% in Foil) and countdown videos show no consistent retention advantage over concise continuous narratives.

Eliminate redundant rephrasing and restatements of the premise; repetitive lines (e.g. Guardrails repeating identical phrasing losing 12.3% at 28%, or Asleep Leg over-explaining circulation losing 9.8% at 26%) cause heavy drop-offs in the 20-35% duration mark.

Do not save the central visual or dramatic experiment for the end; top-retaining videos like 'Could A T. rex Outrun Your Car?' (kept_at_end: 0.507) and 'James Webb' (kept_at_50pct: 0.754) frame a clear comparative scenario right away rather than generic factual trivia.
worst_moment_types: Immediate technical/chemical exposition lines directly following the hook (e.g., sap water percentage, bromelain enzyme, intracellular gas spaces, node structures).
Interactive guessing interruptions and countdowns ('Pause and guess...', 'three, two, one').
Redundant restatements of the opening premise or over-qualifying statements (e.g., repeated vehicle impact lines, dense circulation caveats).
best_hook_types: High-contrast paradoxical comparisons (e.g., 'A bluefin tuna and a cod are both fish, but their meat looks like two completely different animals').
Extreme historical or scale anchors (e.g., 'This shark is older than the United States').
Challenging established astronomical or scientific boundaries (e.g., 'Pluto seemed like our solar system's edge, yet astronomers are investigating...').
